text: You've covered four dense lessons. Before chapter 2 builds qubits and Dirac notation on top of all this, this lab works through a handful of applied scenarios — the kind a colleague might actually ask you about on the spot.

First scenario: could a classical simulation reproduce the double-slit interference pattern just by not bothering to log which slit each particle used? No. In that simulation, each particle genuinely goes through exactly one slit the whole time, logged or not. Real interference comes from the amplitude genuinely covering both paths at once, with no definite single-path fact anywhere in the underlying model — not from a bookkeeping choice layered on top of trajectories that were already definite.

Second scenario: matching postulates to facts about a measured qubit. Why did you get exactly 0 or 1 and nothing in between? Postulates two and three — the observable is Hermitian, so its only possible outcomes are its eigenvalues. Why could you only predict a probability beforehand, not the outcome itself? Postulate three, the Born rule — that's the most quantum mechanics promises about any single trial. And why did an immediate second measurement give the exact same result with certainty? Postulate four — the first measurement already collapsed the state, so there's nothing left to produce a different answer.

Third, the photoelectric effect's threshold behavior, blackbody radiation, and atomic spectral lines are grouped together because they're the same underlying fact — energy isn't continuously divisible at this scale — showing up in three different experimental settings. Fourth, against the claim that skipping the hydrogen atom means this isn't real quantum mechanics: the five postulates themselves are the actual content of quantum mechanics, and the hydrogen atom is just one application of them to a specific physical system. Quantum circuits only ever need postulate one, the state, and postulate five, unitary gates — skipping an application is not the same as skipping the theory.

Put it all together and you get the throughline for this course: classical physics assumed continuous, divisible energy and definite trajectories; a classical bit inherits that comfort. Quantum mechanics showed nature doesn't work that way, and the postulates turned that into precise rules. Chapter 2 starts building the qubit itself on exactly this foundation.
